text:
Shinto - Wikipedia
Contents
Shinto
Shinto
(
Japanese
:
神道
,
Hepburn
:
Shintō
;
Japanese pronunciation:
[
ɕiꜜn.toː
]
[
2
]
)
, also called
Shintoism
, is a
religion
from
Japan
. Classified as an
East Asian religion
by
scholars of religion
, it is often regarded by its practitioners as Japan's
indigenous religion
and as a
nature religion
. Scholars sometimes call its practitioners
Shintoists
, although adherents rarely use that term themselves. With no central authority in control of Shinto, there is much diversity of belief and practice evident among practitioners.
A
polytheistic
and
animistic
religion, Shinto revolves around supernatural entities called the
kami
(
神
), who are believed to inhabit all things, including forces of nature and prominent landscape locations. The
kami
are worshipped at
kamidana
household shrines, family shrines, and
jinja
public shrines
. The latter are staffed by priests, known as
kannushi
, who oversee offerings of food and drink to the specific
kami
enshrined at that location. This is done to cultivate harmony between humans and
kami
and to solicit the latter's blessing. Other common rituals include the
kagura
dances,
rites of passage
, and
kami
festivals
. Public shrines facilitate forms of
divination
and supply religious objects, such as
amulets
, to the religion's adherents. Shinto places a major conceptual focus on ensuring purity, largely by cleaning practices such as ritual washing and bathing, especially before worship. Little emphasis is placed on specific moral codes or particular afterlife beliefs, although the dead are deemed capable of becoming
kami
. The religion has no single creator or specific doctrine, and instead exists in a diverse range of local and regional forms.
Although historians debate at what point it is suitable to refer to Shinto as a distinct religion,
kami
veneration has been traced back to Japan's
Yayoi period
(300 BCE to 250 CE).
Buddhism
entered Japan at the end of the
Kofun period
(300 to 538 CE) and spread rapidly.
Religious syncretization
made
kami
worship and Buddhism functionally inseparable, a process called
shinbutsu-shūgō
. The
kami
came to be viewed as part of
Buddhist cosmology
and were increasingly depicted
anthropomorphically
. The earliest written tradition regarding
kami
worship was recorded in the 8th-century
Kojiki
and
Nihon Shoki
. In ensuing centuries,
shinbutsu-shūgō
was adopted by Japan's Imperial household. During the
Meiji era
(1868 to 1912), Japan's
nationalist
leadership expelled Buddhist influence from
kami
worship and formed
State Shinto
, which some historians regard as the origin of Shinto as a distinct religion. Shrines came under growing government influence, and citizens were encouraged to worship the
emperor
as a
kami
. With the formation of the
Empire of Japan
in the early 20th century, Shinto was exported to other areas of East Asia. Following Japan's defeat in
World War II
, Shinto was formally
separated from the state
.
Shinto is primarily found in Japan, where there are around 100,000 public shrines, although practitioners are also found abroad. Numerically, it is Japan's largest religion, the second being Buddhism. Most of the country's population takes part in both Shinto and Buddhist activities, especially festivals, reflecting a common view in
Japanese culture
that the beliefs and practices of different religions do not need to be exclusive. Aspects of Shinto have been incorporated into various
Japanese new religious movements
.
Definition
There is no universally agreed definition of Shinto.
[
3
]
According to Joseph Cali and John Dougill, if there was "one single, broad definition of Shinto" that could be proposed, it would be that "Shinto is a belief in
kami
", the supernatural entities at the centre of the religion.
[
4
]
The Japanologist
Helen Hardacre
wrote that "Shinto encompasses doctrines, institutions, ritual, and communal life based on
kami
worship",
[
5
]
while the
scholar of religion
Inoue Nobutaka
observed that the term "Shinto" was "often used" in "reference to
kami
worship and related theologies, rituals and practices".
[
6
]
The term
Shinto
is often broadly translated into English as "the way of the
kami
",
[
7
]
although its meaning has varied throughout Japanese history.
[
8
]
In English, the religion is also called "Shintoism",
[
9
]
[
10
]
[
11
]
although some scholars have argued against the inclusion of the suffix
-ism
due to Shinto's lack of codified doctrine.
[
12
]
[
13
]
Various scholars have referred to practitioners of Shinto as
Shintoists
, although this term has no direct translation in the
Japanese language
.
[
14
]
Scholars have debated at what point in history it is legitimate to start talking about Shinto as a specific phenomenon. The scholar of religion
Ninian Smart
suggested that one could "speak of the
kami
religion of Japan, which lived symbiotically with organized Buddhism, and only later was institutionalized as Shinto."
[
15
]
While several institutions and practices now associated with Shinto existed in Japan by the 8th century,
[
16
]
various scholars have argued that Shinto as a distinct religion was essentially "invented" during the 19th century, in Japan's
Meiji era
.
[
17
]
The scholar of religion Brian Bocking stressed that, especially when dealing with periods before the Meiji era, the term
Shinto
should "be approached with caution".
[
18
]
Inoue Nobutaka stated that "Shinto cannot be considered as a single religious system that existed from the ancient to the modern period",
[
19
]
while the historian
Kuroda Toshio
noted that "before modern times Shinto did not exist as an independent religion".
[
20
]
Many scholars describe Shinto as a
religion
,
[
21
]
a term first translated into Japanese as
shūkyō
around the time of the
Meiji Restoration
.
[
22
]
Some practitioners instead view Shinto as a "way",
[
23
]
thus characterising it more as custom or
tradition
,
[
24
]
partly as an attempt to circumvent the modern
separation of religion and state
and restore Shinto's historical links with the Japanese state.
[
25
]
Moreover, many of the categories of religion developed in Western culture "do not readily apply" to Shinto.
[
26
]
Unlike religions familiar in Western countries, such as
Christianity
and
Islam
, Shinto has no single founder,
[
27
]
nor any single canonical text.
[
28
]
Western religions tend to stress exclusivity, but in Japan, it has long been considered acceptable to practice different religions simultaneously.
[
29
]
Japanese religion is therefore highly
pluralistic
.
[
30
]
Shinto is often cited alongside
Buddhism
as one of Japan's two main religions,
[
31
]
and the two often differ in focus, with Buddhism emphasising the idea of the cessation of suffering, while Shinto focuses on adapting to life's pragmatic requirements.
[
32
]
Shinto has integrated elements from religions imported from mainland Asia, such as Buddhism,
Confucianism
,
Taoism
, and
Chinese divination
practices,
[
33
]
and shares features like its polytheism with other
East Asian religions
.
[
34
]
Some scholars suggest we talk about types of Shintō such as popular Shintō, folk Shintō, domestic Shintō, sectarian Shintō, imperial house Shintō, shrine Shintō, state Shintō, new Shintō religions, etc. rather than regard Shintō as a single entity. This approach can be helpful but begs the question of what is meant by 'Shintō' in each case, particularly since each category incorporates or has incorporated Buddhist, Confucian, Taoist, folk religious and other elements.
Scholars of religion have debated how to classify Shinto. Inoue considered it part of "the family of East-Asian religions".
[
36
]
The philosopher
Stuart D. B. Picken
suggested that Shinto be classed as a
world religion
,
[
37
]
while the historian
H. Byron Earhart
called it a "major religion".
[
38
]
Shinto is often described as an
indigenous religion
,
[
39
]
although this generates debates over the different definitions of "indigenous" in the Japanese context.
[
40
]
The notion of Shinto as Japan's "indigenous religion" stemmed from the growth of modern nationalism between the
Edo
and Meiji periods;
[
41
]
this view promoted the idea that Shinto's origins were prehistoric and that it represented something like the "underlying will of Japanese culture".
[
42
]
The prominent Shinto theologian Sokyo Ono, for instance, said
kami
worship was "an expression" of the Japanese "native racial faith which arose in the mystic days of remote antiquity" and that it was "as indigenous as the people that brought the Japanese nation into existence".
[
43
]
Many scholars regard this classification as inaccurate. Earhart noted that Shinto, in having absorbed much Chinese and Buddhist influence, was "too complex to be labelled simply [as an] indigenous religion".
[
38
]
In the early 21st century it became increasingly common for practitioners to call Shinto a
nature religion
,
[
44
]
which critics saw as a strategy to disassociate the tradition from controversial issues surrounding militarism and imperialism.
[
44
]
Shinto displays substantial local variation;
[
45
]
the anthropologist John K. Nelson noted it was "not a unified, monolithic entity".
[
40
]
Different types of Shinto
have been identified. "Shrine Shinto" refers to practices centred around shrines,
[
46
]
and "Domestic Shinto" to the veneration of
kami
in the home.
[
47
]
Some scholars have used the term "Folk Shinto" to designate localised Shinto practices,
[
48
]
or practices outside of an institutionalised setting.
[
40
]
In various past eras, there was also a "
State Shinto
", in which Shinto beliefs and practices were closely interlinked with the Japanese state.
[
46
]
In representing "a portmanteau term" for many varied traditions across Japan, the term "Shinto" is similar to the term "
Hinduism
", used to describe varied traditions across South Asia.
[
49
]
Beliefs
Shinto is
polytheistic
, involving the veneration of deities known as
kami
,
[
50
]
or sometimes as
jingi
(神祇).
[
51
]
In Japanese, the term
kami
refers both to individual
kami
and the collective group of
kami
.
[
52
]
Although lacking a direct English translation,
[
53
]
the term
kami
has sometimes been rendered as "god" or "spirit".
[
54
]
The historian of religion
Joseph Kitagawa
deemed these English translations "quite unsatisfactory and misleading",
[
55
]
and various scholars urge against translating
kami
into English.
[
56
]
In Japanese, it is often said that there are eight million
kami
, a term which connotes an infinite number,
[
57
]
and Shinto practitioners believe that they are present everywhere.
[
5
]
They are not regarded as
omnipotent
,
omniscient
, or necessarily
immortal
.
[
58
]
The term
kami
is "conceptually fluid",
[
59
]
and in Japanese it also applies to the power of phenomena that inspire a sense of wonder and awe.
[
60
]
Kitagawa referred to this as "the
kami
nature", suggesting it was "somewhat analogous" to the Western concepts of the
numinous
and the
sacred
.
[
55
]
Kami
are seen to inhabit both the living and the dead, organic and inorganic matter, and natural disasters like earthquakes, droughts, and plagues;
[
4
]
their presence is seen in natural forces such as the wind, rain, fire, and sunshine.
[
61
]
Accordingly, Nelson commented that Shinto regards "the
actual phenomena
of the world itself" as being "divine".
[
62
]
This perspective has been characterised as
animistic
.
[
63
]
Kami
have been venerated since prehistory.
[
5
]
During the
Yayoi period
they were deemed formless and invisible,
[
64
]
but came to be depicted anthropomorphically under Buddhist influence.
[
65
]
Modern statues of the
kami
are known as
shinzo
.
[
66
]
Kami
are usually associated with a specific place, often a prominent landscape feature such as a waterfall, mountain, large rock, or tree.
[
67
]
Physical objects or places in which the
kami
have a presence are termed
shintai
;
[
68
]
objects inhabited by the
kami
that are placed in the shrine are known as
go-shintai
.
[
69
]
Objects commonly chosen for this purpose include mirrors, swords, stones, beads, and inscribed tablets.
[
70
]
These
go-shintai
are concealed from the view of visitors,
[
71
]
and may be hidden inside boxes so that even the priests do not know what they look like.
[
68
]
Kami
are capable of both benevolent and destructive deeds;
[
72
]
if warnings about good conduct are ignored, the
kami
can mete out punishment, often illness or sudden death, called
shinbatsu
.
[
73
]
Some
kami
, referred to as the
magatsuhi-no-kami
or
araburu kami
, are regarded as malevolent and destructive.
[
74
]
Offerings and prayers are given to the
kami
to gain their blessings and to dissuade them from destructive actions.
[
4
]
Shinto seeks to cultivate and ensure a harmonious relationship between humans and the
kami
and thus with the natural world.
[
75
]
More localised
kami
may be subject to feelings of intimacy and familiarity from members of the local community that are not directed towards more widespread
kami
like Amaterasu.
[
76
]
The
kami
of a particular community is referred to it as their
ujigami
,
[
77
]
while that of a particular house is the
yashikigami
.
[
78
]
Kami
are not considered
metaphysically
different from humanity,
[
59
]
with it being possible for humans to become
kami
.
[
53
]
Ancestors and other dead humans are sometimes venerated as
kami
, being regarded as protectors.
[
79
]
For example,
Emperor Ōjin
was posthumously enshrined as the
kami
Hachiman
, believed to be a protector of Japan and a
kami
of war.
[
80
]
In Western Japan, the term
jigami
is used to describe the enshrined
kami
of a village founder.
[
81
]
In some cases, living human beings were also viewed as
kami
;
[
4
]
these were called
akitsumi kami
[
82
]
or
arahito-gami
.
[
83
]
In the State Shinto system of the Meiji era, the emperor of Japan was declared to be a
kami
,
[
53
]
while several Shinto sects have also viewed their leaders as living
kami
.
[
53
]
Although some
kami
are venerated only in a single location, others have shrines across many areas.
[
84
]
Hachiman for instance has around 25,000 shrines dedicated to him,
[
61
]
while Inari has 40,000.
[
85
]
The act of establishing a new shrine to a
kami
who already has one is called
bunrei
("dividing the spirit").
[
86
]
As part of this, the
kami
is invited to enter a new place, with the instalment ceremony known as a
kanjo
.
[
84
]
The new, subsidiary shrine is known as a
bunsha
.
[
87
]
Individual
kami
are not believed to have their power diminished by their residence in multiple locations, and there is no limit on the number of places a
kami
can be enshrined.
[
84
]
In some periods, fees were charged for the right to enshrine a particular
kami
in a new place.
[
84
]
Shrines are not necessarily always designed as permanent structures.
[
5
]
Many
kami
have messengers, known as
kami no tsukai
or
tsuka washime
, that generally take animal forms.
[
84
]
Inari's messenger, for example, is a fox (
kitsune
),
[
88
]
while Hachiman's is a dove.
[
84
]
Shinto cosmology also includes spirits who cause malevolent acts,
bakemono
, a category including
oni
,
tengu
,
kappa
,
mononoke
, and
yamanba
.
[
89
]
Japanese folklore also incorporates belief in the
goryō
or
onryō
, unquiet or vengeful spirits, particularly of those who died violently and without appropriate funerary rites.
[
90
]
These are believed to inflict suffering on the living, meaning that they must be pacified, usually through Buddhist rites but sometimes through enshrining them as a
kami
.
[
90
]
Other Japanese supernatural figures include the
tanuki
, animal-like creatures who can take human form.
[
91
]
Although the narratives differ in detail,
[
92
]
the origin of the
kami
and of Japan itself are recounted in two 8th-century texts,
Kojiki
and
Nihon Shoki
.
[
93
]
Drawing heavily on Chinese influence,
[
94
]
these texts were commissioned by ruling elites to legitimize and consolidate their rule.
[
95
]
Although never of great importance to Japanese religious life,
[
96
]
in the early 20th century the government proclaimed that their accounts were factual.
[
97
]
The
Kojiki
recounts that the universe started with
ame-tsuchi
, the separation of light and pure elements (
ame
, "heaven") from heavy elements (
tsuchi
, "earth").
[
98
]
Three
kami
then appeared:
Amenominakanushi
,
Takamimusuhi no Mikoto
, and
Kamimusuhi no Mikoto
. Other
kami
followed, including a brother and sister,
Izanagi
and
Izanami
.
[
99
]
The
kami
instructed Izanagi and Izanami to create land on earth. To this end, the siblings stirred the briny sea with a jewelled spear, from which
Onogoro Island
was formed.
[
100
]
Izanagi and Izanami then descended to Earth, where the latter gave birth to further
kami
. One of these was a fire
kami
, whose birth killed Izanami.
[
101
]
Izanagi descended to
yomi
to retrieve his sister, but there he saw her body putrefying. Embarrassed to be seen in this state, she chased him out of
yomi
, and he closed its entrance with a boulder.
[
102
]
Izanagi bathed in the sea to rid himself from the pollution brought about by witnessing Izanami's putrefaction. Through this act, further
kami
emerged from his body:
Amaterasu
(the sun
kami
) was born from his left eye,
Tsukuyomi
(the moon
kami
) from his right eye, and
Susanoo
(the storm
kami
) from his nose.
[
103
]
Susanoo behaved in a destructive manner, so to escape him Amaterasu hid in a cave, plunging the earth into darkness. The other
kami
eventually coaxed her out.
[
104
]
Susanoo was then banished to earth, where he married and had children.
[
105
]
According to the
Kojiki
, Amaterasu then sent her grandson,
Ninigi
, to rule Japan, giving him curved beads, a mirror, and a sword: the symbols of Japanese imperial authority.
[
106
]
Amaterasu remains probably Japan's most venerated
kami
.
[
107
]
In Shinto, the creative principle permeating all life is known as
musubi
, and is associated with its own
kami
.
[
108
]
Traditional Japanese thought has no concept of an overarching duality between good and evil;
[
109
]
the concept of
aki
encompasses misfortune, unhappiness, and disaster, although it does not correspond precisely with the Western concept of evil.
[
110
]
There is no
eschatology
in Shinto.
[
111
]
Texts such as the
Kojiki
and
Nihon Shoki
portray multiple realms in Shinto cosmology.
[
112
]
These present a universe divided into three parts: the Plane of High Heaven (
Takama-no-hara
), where the
kami
live; the Phenomenal or Manifested World (
Utsushi-yo
), where humans dwell; and the Nether World (
Yomotsu-kuni
), where unclean spirits reside.
[
113
]
The mythological texts nevertheless do not draw firm demarcations between these realms.
[
114
]
Modern Shinto places greater emphasis on this life than on any afterlife,
[
115
]
although it does espouse belief in a human spirit or soul, the
mitama
or
tamashii
, which contains four aspects.
[
116
]
While indigenous ideas about an afterlife were probably well-developed prior to Buddhism's arrival,
[
117
]
contemporary Japanese people often adopt Buddhist afterlife beliefs.
[
118
]
Mythological stories like the
Kojiki
describe
yomi
or
yomi-no-kuni
as a realm of the dead,
[
119
]
although this plays no role in modern Shinto.
[
117
]
Modern Shinto ideas about the afterlife largely revolve around the idea that the spirit survives bodily death and continues to assist the living. After 33 years, it then becomes part of the family
kami
.
[
120
]
These ancestral spirits are sometimes thought to reside in the mountains,
[
121
]
from where they descend to take part in agricultural events.
[
122
]
Shinto's afterlife beliefs also include the
obake
, restless spirits who died in bad circumstances and often seek revenge.
[
123
]
A key theme in Shinto is the avoidance of
kegare
("pollution" or "impurity"),
[
124
]
while ensuring
harae
("purity").
[
125
]
In Japanese thought, humans are seen as fundamentally pure.
[
126
]
Kegare
is therefore seen as a temporary condition that can be corrected through achieving
harae
.
[
127
]
Rites of purification are performed to restore an individual to "spiritual" health and render them useful to society.
[
128
]
This notion of purity is present in many facets of Japanese culture, such as the focus it places on bathing.
[
129
]
Purification is for instance regarded as important in preparation for the planting season,
[
130
]
while performers of
noh
theatre undergo a purification rite before they carry out their performances.
[
131
]
Among the things regarded as particular pollutants in Shinto are death, disease, witchcraft, the flaying alive of an animal, incest, bestiality, excrement, and blood associated with either menstruation or childbirth.
[
132
]
To avoid
kegare
, priests and other practitioners may engage in abstinence and avoid various activities prior to a festival or ritual.
[
133
]
Various words, termed
imi-kotoba
, are also regarded as taboo, and people avoid speaking them when at a shrine; these include
shi
(death),
byō
(illness), and
shishi
(meat).
[
134
]
A purification ceremony known as
misogi
involves the use of fresh water, salt water, or salt to remove
kegare
.
[
135
]
Full immersion in the sea is often regarded as the most ancient and efficacious form of purification.
[
136
]
This act links with the mythological tale in which Izanagi immersed himself in the sea to purify himself after discovering his deceased wife; it was from this act that other
kami
sprang from his body.
[
137
]
An alternative is immersion beneath a waterfall.
[
138
]
Salt is often regarded as a purifying substance;
[
139
]
some Shinto practitioners will for instance sprinkle salt on themselves after a funeral,
[
140
]
while those running restaurants may put a small pile of salt outside before business commences each day.
[
141
]
Fire, also, is perceived as a source of purification.
[
142
]
The
yaku-barai
is a form of harae designed to prevent misfortune,
[
143
]
while the
oharae
, or "ceremony of great purification", is often used for end-of-year purification rites, and is conducted twice a year at many shrines.
[
144
]
Shinto incorporates morality tales and myths but no codified ethical doctrine,
[
4
]
and thus no systematised code of behavior.
[
28
]
An ethical system nevertheless arises from its practice,
[
145
]
with emphasis placed on sincerity (
makoto
),
[
146
]
honesty (
tadashii
),
[
147
]
hard work (
tsui-shin
),
[
148
]
and thanksgiving (
kansha
) directed towards the
kami
.
[
148
]
Shojiki
is regarded as a virtue, encompassing honesty, uprightness, veracity, and frankness.
[
149
]
Shinto sometimes includes reference to four virtues known as the
akaki kiyoki kokoro
or
sei-mei-shin
, meaning "purity and cheerfulness of heart", which are linked to the state of
harae
.
[
150
]
Attitudes to sex and fertility tend to be forthright in Shinto.
[
151
]
Shinto's flexibility regarding morality has been a target of criticism, especially from those arguing that the religion can readily become a pawn for powerful people to legitimise their authority.
[
152
]
In Shinto,
kannagara
("way of the
kami
") is the law of the
natural order
,
[
147
]
with
wa
("
benign harmony
") being inherent in all things.
[
153
]
Disrupting
wa
is deemed bad, while contributing to it is thought good;
[
154
]
as such, subordination of the individual to the larger social unit has long been a characteristic of the religion.
[
155
]
Throughout Japanese history, the notion of
saisei-itchi
, or the union of religious authority and political authority, has long been prominent.
[
156
]
In the modern world, Shinto has tended toward conservatism,
[
157
]
as well as nationalism,
[
158
]
an association that results in various Japanese
civil liberties
groups and neighboring countries regarding Shinto suspiciously.
[
159
]
Particularly controversial has been the
Yasukuni Shrine
in Tokyo, devoted to Japan's war dead. In 1979 it enshrined 14 men who had been declared Class-A defendants at the 1946
Tokyo War Crimes Trials
, generating domestic and international condemnation, particularly from China and Korea.
[
160
]
Shinto priests face ethical conundrums. In the 1980s, for instance, priests at the
Suwa Shrine
in
Nagasaki
debated whether to invite the crew of a U.S. Navy vessel docked at the port city to their festival celebrations given the sensitivities surrounding the
1945 U.S. use of the atomic bomb on the city
.
[
161

Shinto
focuses on ritual behavior rather than doctrine
.
[
168
]
The philosophers James W. Boyd and Ron G. Williams stated that Shinto is "first and foremost a ritual tradition",
[
169
]
while Picken observed that "Shinto is interested not in
credenda
but in
agenda
, not in things that should be believed but in things that should be done."
[
170
]
The scholar of religion Clark B. Offner stated that Shinto's focus was on "maintaining communal, ceremonial traditions for the purpose of human (communal) well-being".
[
171
]
It is often difficult to distinguish Shinto practices from Japanese customs more broadly,
[
172
]
with Picken observing that the "worldview of Shinto" provided the "principal source of self-understanding within the Japanese way of life".

Nelson stated that "Shinto-based orientations and values

Public spaces in which the
kami
are worshipped are often known under the generic term
jinja
("
kami
-place");
[
174
]
this term applies to the location rather than to a specific building.
[
175
]
Jinja
is usually translated as "shrine" in English,
[
176
]
although in earlier literature was sometimes translated as "temple",
[
14
]
a term now more commonly reserved for Japan's Buddhist structures.
[
177
]
There are around 100,000 public shrines in Japan;
[
178
]
about 80,000 are affiliated with the
Association of Shinto Shrines
,
[
179
]
with another 20,000 being unaffiliated.
[
180
]
They are found all over the country, from isolated rural areas to dense metropolitan ones.
[
181
]
More specific terms are sometimes used for certain shrines depending on their function; some of the grand shrines with imperial associations are termed
jingū
,
[
182
]
those devoted to the war dead are termed
shokonsha
,
[
149
]
and those linked to mountains deemed to be inhabited by
kami
are
yama-miya
.
[
183
]
Jinja typically consist of complexes of multiple buildings,
[
184
]
with the architectural styles of shrines having largely developed by the
Heian period
.
[
185

The inner sanctuary in which the
kami
lives is the
honden
.
[
186
]
Inside the
honden
may be stored material belonging to the
kami
; known as
shinpo
, this can include artworks, clothing, weapons, musical instruments, bells, and mirrors.
[
187
]
Typically, worshippers carry out their acts outside of the
honden
.
[
31
]
Near the
honden
can sometimes be found a subsidiary shrine, the
bekkū
, to another
kami
; the
kami
inhabiting this shrine is not necessarily perceived as being inferior to that in the
honden
.
[
188
]
At some places, halls of worship have been erected, termed
haiden
.
[
189
]
On a lower level can be found the hall of offerings, known as a
heiden
.
[
190
]
Together, the building housing the
honden
,
haiden
, and
heiden
is called a
hongū
.
[
191
]
In some shrines, there is a separate building in which to conduct additional ceremonies, such as weddings, known as a
gishikiden
,
[
192
]
or a specific building in which the
kagura

Collectively, the central buildings of a shrine are known as the
shaden
,

194
]

keidaichi
[

Shrine entrances are marked by a two-post gateway with either one or two crossbeams atop it, known as

199
]
The exact details of these
torii
varies and there are at least twenty different styles.

200
]
These are regarded as demarcating the area where the
kami
resides;
[
31
]
passing under them is often viewed as a form of purification.

201
]
More broadly,

are internationally recognised symbols of Japan.
[
31

Their architectural form is distinctly Japanese, although the decision to paint most of them in
vermillion
